analysis.one_liner: Raises the cap on civil fines for violating federal product safety laws from $1.25 million to $10 million.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill by voice vote in October 2007, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended, leaving the penalty cap unchanged at $1.25 million.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies that sell hazardous or defective products in the United States can be fined under three federal safety laws, but the maximum fine was $1.25 million—an amount large firms can treat as a business cost. This bill raises that cap to $10 million and requires the Consumer Product Safety Commission to weigh how serious a violation was when setting the fine. The House passed it without a recorded objection; the Senate committee where it landed never brought it to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who rely on the Consumer Product Safety Commission to police unsafe toys, textiles, and household goods. Stronger fines give the agency more leverage to penalize companies that knowingly sell dangerous products, and the House-passed version set an interim $5 million cap that would take effect within about a year of enactment [S3][S4].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the maximum civil penalty under the Consumer Product Safety Act, the Federal Hazardous Substances Act, and the Flammable Fabrics Act from $1.25 million to $10 million [S3][S4].
Requires the Commission to consider the nature, circumstances, extent, and gravity of a violation when setting a penalty, and to issue a regulation interpreting those factors [S4].
Provides a temporary $5 million cap effective within roughly a year of enactment, before the permanent $10 million cap takes effect [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers and importers of consumer products, textiles, and hazardous substances, who face fines up to eight times the prior cap for safety violations. Costs ultimately can be passed to consumers through prices.

drawbacks.text: An eight-fold increase in the maximum fine raises the cost of violating safety rules for product makers, a cost that can be passed through to consumers in prices.

The bill directs the Commission to weigh the gravity of a violation but leaves the agency itself to define those penalty factors by regulation, adding regulatory discretion that affected companies would have to navigate [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a narrow problem: a maximum fine of $1.25 million is small relative to the revenue of large manufacturers, so it can be absorbed as a cost of doing business rather than deterrence. Raising the cap mainly affects companies that commit serious or repeated violations; the direct public benefit is a stronger deterrent against selling dangerous products, and the direct cost is higher compliance and penalty exposure for industry.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote in October 2007, but the Senate Commerce Committee referred it and never acted before the Congress ended in January 2009 [S6].

narrative.text: Introduced May 24, 2007 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which held subcommittee and full committee markups and reported the bill as amended in September 2007 [S6].
The House passed the amended bill by voice vote under suspension of the rules on October 9, 2007 [S6].
The Senate received the bill on October 15, 2007 and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, where no further action was taken before the 110th Congress ended [S1][S6].

The bill's outcome mirrors a familiar pattern of the period: legislation raising product safety penalties and strengthening the Consumer Product Safety Commission was folded into the broader Consumer Product Safety Improvement Act enacted in 2008, after the 2007 recall wave of lead-tainted toys, rather than moving as a stand-alone bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Product manufacturers and importers benefit from the bill's failure: the $1.25 million penalty cap remained in place, keeping the maximum legal exposure for safety violations far below what the House had approved. Consumers gained nothing directly, though Congress later raised penalties through separate product safety legislation the following year.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Product makers who kept the old fine cap

for.name: Rep. Bobby L. Rush
for.role: Sponsor and chair of the House subcommittee with jurisdiction over consumer protection
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, chaired its subcommittee markup, and moved in the House to suspend the rules and pass the bill as amended.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Held hearings and markups, ordered the bill reported amended by voice vote, and reported it with House Report 110-364.

for.name: The House
for.what_they_did: Agreed to the bill by voice vote on October 9, 2007 with no recorded opposition.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction in the Senate
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on October 15, 2007 and took no action—no hearing, markup, or floor report—before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No recorded votes exist: the House passed the bill by voice vote with no visible opposition, and the Senate never voted, so the partisan shape of the delay cannot be measured from the record [S6].

industries.note: The bill raises the maximum civil fine for safety violations from $1.25 million to $10 million, and its interest in blocking the bill ran against consumers, who benefit from stronger deterrence against selling dangerous products [S3][S4].
The bill raises the penalty cap under the Flammable Fabrics Act to $10 million for violations involving flammable fabrics [S3][S4].
